title: Throwing a stoneware storage crock
subtitle: Throwing and trimming a wide-mouthed stoneware crock for dry goods storage
excerpt: A storage crock is one of the most functional forms in the pottery kitchen: wide-mouthed, thick-walled, stable on its base. This pattern throws a 1.5-litre capacity crock in smooth stoneware, trims a foot ring and a recessed lid seat, and specifies the wall thickness and proportion needed for the form to survive daily use.
sourceNotes: Storage crock form is a classic utilitarian stoneware piece. Proportions and wall thickness specifications derived from functional ceramics best practice.

glossaryTerms.definition: The first wheel step: working the clay mass until it runs true with no wobble at any speed.
Pressing the centred clay downward and outward to form the floor of the vessel, before pulling up walls.
Raising the clay walls by squeezing the clay upward from base to rim in a series of passes.
The correct drying stage for trimming: the clay holds its shape but a tool still cuts it cleanly.
A trimmed recessed base that raises the vessel from the shelf, allowing glazing of the bottom and a stable flat base after firing.

content.text: This pattern requires a pottery wheel, a kiln firing to cone 6 (approximately 1220 °C), and glazing with a food-safe mid-fire glaze. Confirm your kiln is calibrated to reach the specified cone before beginning. Use a witness cone on each firing to verify temperature.

A storage crock works best in stoneware rather than earthenware: the fully-vitrified body is dense, non-porous, and resists chipping from daily handling better than lower-fire clays. The form is straightforward: a cylinder that widens slightly above the base, with thick walls (7 to 8 mm) for thermal mass and durability. A lid seat is trimmed into the rim during throwing, recessed by 5 mm to seat a thrown or slab lid.
Prepare the clay and wedge
Weigh out 1,100 g of smooth stoneware. Wedge thoroughly: 50 turns minimum: until no air pockets remain. Form into a rounded cone before placing on the wheel bat.
Throwing the crock
Centre the clay on the wheel bat.
Centring

is complete when the clay does not wobble at medium speed (30 rpm) with your hands resting on the sides. For a storage crock, centring must be true: off-centre clay in a thick-walled form exaggerates the wobble through every subsequent pull.

Open the clay by pressing your dominant thumb downward into the centre, stopping 10 mm above the wheel bat: this becomes the floor thickness. Press outward to form the floor of the crock to 14 cm interior diameter.
Opening
should leave even floor thickness throughout: check by pressing a needle tool from outside the base and marking the depth.
Pull up the walls in three to four passes. For each
pull

: inside hand pinches from the inside at the base; outside hand supports and compresses from outside. Move both hands upward together at the same rate: uneven pace thins walls unevenly. The target wall thickness at the mid-point is 7 to 8 mm.

The crock form: straight-sided cylinder that widens by 2 to 3 cm from base to rim. Keep the rim straight for the lid seat. Final interior height approximately 14 cm; interior diameter at the rim 15 to 16 cm.

Trim the lid seat into the rim: use a wooden rib to compress the rim flat, then hold a small metal rib at the inside edge and push inward by 5 mm while the wheel turns slowly, creating a recessed step for the lid to rest on. Measure the interior rim diameter with calipers and note for matching the lid.
Cut from the wheel bat with a wire cutter. Leave on the bat undisturbed until leather-hard.
Trimming the foot ring
At
leather-hard

(8 to 12 hours after throwing in a normal workshop environment), flip the crock upside-down and centre it on the wheel. Secure with three small clay pads placed evenly around the rim, pressing them to the wheel bat to hold the crock steady.
Trim a
foot ring

using a loop tool: mark the outer and inner edges of the foot ring on the base with a needle tool while the wheel turns. The foot ring should be 3 to 4 mm wide and 5 mm tall. Remove clay from inside the foot ring first, then refine the outer edge.
Check the base weight by lifting: a storage crock base should feel solid but not excessively thick. Aim for 8 to 10 mm base thickness. Trim further if the base feels heavy relative to the walls.
Drying, bisque, and glaze firing

Dry slowly under plastic for 24 hours, then uncovered for a further 24 to 48 hours until fully bone-dry. Bisque fire to cone 06 (approximately 1000 °C). Glaze the interior and exterior except the foot ring with a food-safe mid-fire glaze. Glaze fire to cone 6 (approximately 1220 °C).

rows.cause: Uneven wall thickness around the rim; one side pulled more than the other
rows.fix: Use a wooden rib to compress the rim back to round. Rotate slowly at low speed and apply equal pressure on both sides.

rows.problem: Lid seat step is uneven depth around the rim
rows.cause: Metal rib pressure not consistent through the full rotation
rows.fix: Use calipers to check the lid seat depth at four points around the rim. Re-trim the shallowest sections while still leather-hard.

rows.problem: Base too thick after trimming: crock feels heavy
rows.cause: Opening did not go deep enough; floor retained too much clay
rows.fix: Trim further with the loop tool from the inside of the foot ring. Do not trim below 8 mm base thickness or the base becomes fragile at firing.
